title: Ukraine's proposed post-martial-law minimum-wage path is a formal-recovery bargain between earnings, jobs, and social-contribution capacity
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11443, Minimum Wage Reform in a Wartime Economy: Simulating Impacts from Ukraine's Proposed Reform, September 2026
geography: Ukraine; formal private-sector and nonmilitary public-sector workers, employers, low-wage workers, social-insurance institutions, and post-martial-law reconstruction policy

denominator.unit: 10 percent random sample of 2023 Pension Fund of Ukraine worker-level data covering jobs with pension contributions

proposal.value: the simulated proposal sets the minimum wage at 40% of the previous year's average wage after martial law and raises it by two percentage points annually until 50%

data_scope.value: the sample covers private-sector and nonmilitary public-sector jobs with pension contributions

counterfactual.value: the reform is compared with a path adjusted only for wage inflation

observations.method: Forward-looking microsimulation using a 10% random sample of Pension Fund administrative worker-level data and a proposed five-year transition path.
observations.uncertainty: The proposal is simulated rather than implemented; results depend on wage, employment, compliance, and transition assumptions and exclude workers outside the covered formal-sector data.
observations.subgroup: Low-wage formal workers, employers, private and nonmilitary public sectors, workers outside pension-contribution systems, and social-insurance institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: A wage floor can strengthen household purchasing power and formal contribution bases, while even modest job losses may be concentrated among younger, lower-skilled, smaller-firm, or conflict-exposed workers.

observations.period: Five-year simulated transition; earnings and employment

denominator.unit: World Bank simulation of Ukraine's proposed minimum-wage reform

wage_path.value: by the end of the five-year transition, the simulated minimum wage is 45% above the level reached under wage-inflation-only adjustment

job_losses.value: projected job losses are 0.51% to 1.03% under the simulated proposal
job_losses.unit: percent of covered formal-sector jobs, modeled range

total_earnings.value: total earnings increase by up to 3.24% in the simulation

observations.method: Administrative-data-based simulation of direct and indirect wage, employment, and earnings effects across the transition period.
observations.uncertainty: These are model outputs, not observed effects; they do not account for all post-war labour reallocation, informal work, employer adjustment, migration, inflation, or enforcement responses.
observations.subgroup: Workers near the wage floor, employers with different wage structures, sectors with different labour demand, and workers moving between formal and informal employment.
observations.counterinterpretation: Aggregate earnings gains can coexist with concentrated job loss or reduced hiring, making distribution and transition support as important as the average result.

observations.period: Five-year simulated transition; fiscal and social-contract channel

contribution_channel.value: social contributions and taxes change in the same direction as earnings because they are fixed percentages of earnings in Ukraine

recovery_bargain.value: the proposed wage path links household earnings, employer costs, employment, and social-insurance financing during post-war recovery

policy_tool.value: the methodology is presented as a tool for anticipating likely effects of wage reform on formal workers and public finances

observations.method: World Bank microsimulation linking worker earnings, employment, social contributions, and taxes under a formal-sector wage-floor scenario.
observations.uncertainty: The model does not establish political acceptance, compliance, informal-sector spillovers, realized tax collection, or whether higher wages improve household welfare after prices and war-related costs.
observations.subgroup: Formal workers, employers, taxpayers, social-insurance beneficiaries, informal workers, and households exposed to wartime inflation and displacement.
observations.counterinterpretation: A formal wage floor can improve state capacity and household room, but if enforcement is weak or firms exit formality, the contribution channel may not materialize.

boundary: This record adds a post-war wage-floor route linking formal earnings, modeled employment, social contributions, taxes, household room, and reconstruction legitimacy. It is a simulation of a proposed reform, not an observed policy effect, and does not establish informal-sector impacts, political acceptance, compliance, inflation-adjusted welfare, or universal job quality.
